🚨🇲🇽 <u>Chihuahua's Former Prosecutor Arrested in the CIA Case</u>

César Jáuregui, Maru Campos's former state prosecutor, was arrested in Chihuahua on Saturday. A judge approved warrants on October 16 for him and for Guillermo Zuany, former head of the state's anti-kidnapping unit, on charges of unlawful exercise of public service and giving false statements to authorities. The case goes back to April 19, when a crash in the Chihuahua sierra killed two US agents later identified as CIA, along with two state investigators. The next day Jáuregui went on air to say only Mexican forces took part in the raid: about 40 soldiers and 40 state agents.

🇲🇽🛢️ <u>With Oil Over $100, Mexico Puts Nearly 10 Pesos a Liter Back Into Diesel</u>

For October 17-23, Hacienda zeroes out the IEPS fuel tax on diesel for the sixth straight week, a discount of 7.36 pesos per liter, and more than doubles the complementary stimulus from 1.09 to 2.35 pesos. That comes to 9.72 pesos per liter, El Economista reports. Gasoline gets less help this week: the IEPS rises to 2.71 pesos per liter on Magna and 1.91 on Premium. Sener says the voluntary price agreement holds, keeping regular gasoline below 24 pesos a liter and diesel below 27.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Morena Moves to Put Jalisco's Governor on Political Trial for Repression</u>

Morena state deputies Mariana Casillas and Alejandro Puerto will file for a political trial (juicio político) against Movimiento Ciudadano governor Pablo Lemus before the federal Congress. The trigger was October 11, when Guadalajara residents marched for clean water and got water cannons and tear gas. Puerto called the police crackdown and arrests "a state crime." The filing will also cite the January repression of transit-fare protests and the November 2025 crackdown over water shortages.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>Mexico Arrests "El Trébol," Wanted in Texas, at Querétaro's Airport</u>

Mexican federal forces arrested Erick Eduardo Ríos Estrada, alias "el Trébol" or "Chilangolandia," near Querétaro International Airport. He is accused of belonging to a transnational cell that moved cocaine and methamphetamine into Texas. The operation was run by the SSPC, the FGR, the Criminal Investigation Agency and Interpol México. The DEA shared information. Mexican agents did the surveillance and made the arrest, and the extradition order from the Southern District of Texas now goes before Mexico's Public Ministry.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>Washington Bans Drones Along the Mexican Border for a Year</u>

The FAA, together with the US Departments of Transportation, War and Homeland Security, is closing the airspace along the border with Mexico to unauthorized drones: from the ground up to 400 feet (122 meters), in a strip one nautical mile deep on the US side. The ban runs from October 19, 2026 to October 19, 2027. Washington says it will protect border-security operations and stop cartel drones.

🇲🇽🐄 <u>Sonora Halts Cattle Exports to the US Over a Suspected Foot-and-Mouth Lesion</u>

Mexican inspectors at the Agua Prieta crossing found a lesion on a US-bound calf that could be confused with foot-and-mouth disease. Sader and Senasica didn't wait for the lab: they suspended live-cattle inspections at the station, sent 1,300 head back to their ranch of origin and shipped a sample to Senasica's laboratory in Mexico City. Mexico has been free of foot-and-mouth since 1954, and the protocol exists to keep it that way. Exports through Chihuahua's San Jerónimo station continue as normal.

🇲🇽🛢️ <u>CFE to Vote on 60+ Wind and Solar Plants Worth $12.5 Billion</u>

Mexico's CFE board votes on October 20 on more than 60 power projects, mostly wind and solar, adding about 8.2 gigawatts to the grid at an estimated cost of $12.5 billion, El Financiero reports, citing Bloomberg. Private firms can partner, but on the state's terms: by law, CFE keeps at least 54% of the country's generation. The plan aims for 32 GW of new capacity by 2030, 40% of it renewable.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Jalisco's Water Utility Is Drowning in Debt While Taps Run Brown</u>

As 520 Guadalajara neighborhoods report foul, brown water, Jalisco's metro water utility SIAPA keeps piling up debt. The Jalisco state government owes it more than 207 million pesos for water going back to 2006. Even so, SIAPA approved a 300-million-peso loan for new meters on October 1, and charged them to users' bills. It's also renegotiating 870.7 million pesos with Banobras and 416.9 million with Banorte. After the October 11 march, which state police broke up with tear gas, Lemus still hasn't said how much of the debt has been paid.

🇲🇽🏭 <u>Mexico Opens Tariff-Free Parts Imports to 11 Automakers, With Strings Attached</u>

Mexico's Economy Ministry says 11 automakers with plants in Mexico can now import parts duty-free to assemble light vehicles under the five-year decree published October 13. They'll need a bonded-warehouse permit, a prior import license, and must report the VIN of every car built with those parts. The ministry will set minimum volumes of complete vehicles built in Mexico, and the goal is to raise national content step by step. The point is to replace finished cars imported from countries with no trade deal with Mexico with cars built here. Until now, this tariff line covered just 0.01% of auto imports.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>Ebrard: The Tariff Talks Aren't Frozen, and Lutnick Never Said No</u>

After a Wall Street Journal report said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had stalled a deal to cut US tariffs on Mexico, Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard told the Chamber of Deputies: "They are not interrupted. That's the first thing I want to be clear about." He said that in every Zoom and phone call, Lutnick "has never told me he opposes reducing the 232." Mexico's ask is simple: Mexican cars and steel shouldn't pay more than what Europe, Japan and Korea pay. "Nobody pays more than 15%."
